geo.title: Get started
geo.body:
Why are triangles rigid but squares wobbly? Bridge truss models; then prove the two halves of a kite congruent.

Goal: I can follow and explain a proof of SSS using SAS and isosceles triangles, covering every case of where the joining segment falls.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html:
SSS: if three sides of one triangle are equal to three sides of another, the triangles are congruent.

Proof (following Jacobs): given triangles ABC and DEF with AB = DE, BC = EF and CA = FD. On the other side of AB from C, copy angle EDF at A and mark AG = DF. Then triangle ABG is congruent to triangle DEF by SAS, so BG = EF = BC and AG = DF = AC. Join C to G. Triangles ACG and BCG are isosceles, so their base angles at C and G are equal. If CG crosses AB between A and B, add the angles; if it passes outside, subtract; if it passes through A or B, use the one isosceles triangle. In every case angle ACB = angle AGB, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ABG by SAS, and so to triangle DEF.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html: Why is a triangle frame rigid but a square frame wobbly?
slides.reveal: SSS: three fixed sides fix the triangle's angles. Four fixed sides do not fix a quadrilateral's angles.
